utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. I was advised that Defence has a matter to raise before we hear evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning. This concerns the witness after the one that we're going to hear now, which is Thomas [sic] Glavas. Unfortunately, because of logistical problems, the UNDU was not able to accommodate an interview between Mr. Glavas and Dr. Karadzic over the weekend, and he wasn't able to arrive any earlier than that. So Mr. Sladojevic did meet with him briefly last night, and we would now ask for a pause of one hour after the testimony of the first witness, in which Mr. Glavas can meet with Dr. Karadzic. In addition, Mr. Karadzic received this morning three documents relating to Mr. Glavas' testimony, two proofing notes and a revised, amalgamated statement, and he hasn't had a chance to look at that yet. But we think that within the hour, we can also accomplish that. So our request is that when we complete the testimony of the first witness today, we take a one-hour recess to accomplish the interview and the review of the new material. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does the Prosecution have an observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just very briefly. I certainly don't want to appear over-strident, since it's a relatively modest request. Nevertheless, I think it's important to underscore that long ago Judge Bonomy emphasised that there is no right to such pre-testimony interviews, and certainly if such a right existed, there wouldn't be an accompanying right for the accused to insist on conducting all the interviews himself. That is why this problem arises, and my understanding is this witness advised VWS, back in September of 2009, that he was prepared to be interviewed. So I think that's the situation we find ourselves in. And why, I leave it to the Court, but I don't think those considerations can be ignored.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that there is a difference between an ordinary accused and the accused who represents him or herself, and I think that is of significance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As Mr. Tieger indicated, given that the request is a modest one, we will accept it. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, could you state your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: My name is Sanija Dzevlan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you previously testify at the Tribunal in the trial of Stanislav Galic?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you yesterday, with the assistance of an interpreter, review a transcript of your evidence in that trial?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I understand you wish to make corrections to one word which appears four times in that transcript, and I'll read that correction into the record. The word "Treskavica" appears four times on pages -- on page 3547, at lines 17 and 18, and at page 3548, at lines 1 and 2. Ms. Dzevlan, I understand that in all four of those locations, you wish to substitute the word "Jahorina" for "Treskavica." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Subject to those corrections, do you adopt that transcript as your evidence in this trial, and if you're questioned today about the same events, would you provide the same information to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, the transcript of the witness's evidence in English is 65 ter 22521, and I tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2291, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And I'll read a brief summary of the witness's evidence for the benefit of the public. During the conflict, Ms. Dzevlan lived in Dobrinja IIIA in Sarajevo. Those living there lived in fear. They could not move around freely, as it was very dangerous, and there were many casualties. Barricades were put up in several locations as protection against sniper fire. The 6th of January, 1994, was a particularly calm day in Dobrinja. As it was calm, Ms. Dzevlan, who was an unarmed civilian, decided to go to a hospital to pick up some medicine to bring to her mother, who was sick at home. While returning home on her bicycle, Ms. Dzevlan crossed a bridge. She was the only passer-by in the area at that time. Barricades extended along the length of the bridge on both sides. Ms. Dzevlan was struck by a bullet, and several other bullets landed on the road in front of her at the same time. She managed to cycle on to where neighbours helped to take her to a hospital for treatment. Ms. Dzevlan believes that she was fired upon either from an Orthodox Church or from buildings next to the church in Dobrinja IV. Both the church and the neighbouring buildings were under VRS control. On the following day, a man was struck by a bullet while crossing the same bridge. That ends the public summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Ms. Dzevlan, I'm going to go straight to the incident in question, and I'd like to call up 65 ter 20571. Ms. Dzevlan, is that the bridge which you were crossing when you were shot?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, we see several lanes of traffic. For the sake of orientation, those lanes of traffic are on the bridge itself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You were cycling along one of those lanes when you were struck; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, we see, marked with a black marker, some Xs and lines on one side of the bridge. Could you confirm what those markings represent?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: A barricade erected on the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And there was a similar barricade on the other side of the bridge; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The building indicated with a circle is the Orthodox Church; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And the buildings to the left of the church are in Dobrinja IV; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to tell the Court when, exactly, you were struck by the bullet. Was it before you entered the bridge, while you were on the bridge, or as you were exiting the bridge?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: As I was exiting the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And were you knocked off your bicycle by the shot?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, could you describe the visibility in the area at the moment that you were shot?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Well, it was still day-time, because it was impossible to move during night-time because there was no electricity and it was pitch dark. So it was day-time and the visibility was good.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you express -- perhaps in greater detail, when you say "visibility was good," could you give Their Honours a concept of how good it was?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Well, it was still day-time, as I said. One could see, I think. I don't understand your question. Can you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Certainly. You said earlier that visibility was good. Could you express, in a little more detail, how good it was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It's just a suggestion, but one might be able to ask the witness to look at the photograph and see that relative to the degree of visibility that we can see apparent in the photograph, whether it was better or worse than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you understand that question, Ms. Dzevlan?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes, I understood the question. The visibility was more or less like the one that we see here, only it was an overcast day on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The bridge that you were crossing passes over a river; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Was that river a source of water for people in your community at that time?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes, the river water was used for washing, for flushing toilets, and other things because we didn't have any water. That was the only source that we used for washing. We couldn't use it as drinking water.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did people go down to the river at the location of this bridge to get water?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes, they used to go there to fetch water and to wash their laundry on the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, are you aware of any incidents involving the people who would go there to fetch water and to wash their laundry?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes, I know that some of them were wounded, some women were wounded, and I also heard that one of the women was killed under the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How were those women wounded, and how was -- the woman who was killed, how was she killed?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Probably by a sniper bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How, exactly, do you know that? How did you come to hear about the women being wounded and the woman being killed?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Because I lived near to the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you said that -- you suggested that the woman was killed by a sniper bullet. And the women who were wounded, could you clarify, how were they wounded?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I suppose that they were wounded either by the sniper bullet or a burst of fire. I have no knowledge of weapons, so I can't tell you exactly; all I know is that the bullets were fired from rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender the photograph, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2292, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to call up now Exhibit D670, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: While that's coming up, I want to go back to the moment at which you were struck. Do you believe that you were struck after you had exited the area where the barricades stood?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: On the screen in front of you, on the left, do you see a statement which you made on 30th of September, 1994?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in the opening words of the paragraph underneath the word "Statement," do you see the words: "On 6th of January, 1994, at around 1630 hours, I was returning home on my bicycle"?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And you go on to describe the incident. Do you recall that in your testimony in the Galic trial, you said that the incident took place between 3.00 and 4.00?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you explain to Their Honours why you said in this statement that it was 1630 hours when you were returning home on your bicycle?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Well, the statement I gave in September, I would say that it was still daylight at half past 4.00. Unable, due to the shock, to find my bearings around the exact time and what the hour was, I suppose that at one moment I said that it was at 1630, but I couldn't have been sure because I didn't have a watch. I clearly remember that we had lunch on that date -- day and that at around 3.00, I left my home, went to the hospital, and came back, because I knew that it was impossible to move during night-time because there was no electricity and everything was pitch dark. I had a little baby at the time, and I couldn't afford to venture out during night-time and leave my child alone. So it is possible that at the time when I gave this statement, this is what I said, that it was 1630. I do remember, though, that it was a bright day and that I headed for the hospital after lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You mentioned in your answer that you didn't have a watch. Could you clarify, were you wearing a watch at any point on the day that you were struck?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: No, never. When a person gets wounded, it just never crosses his or her mind to look at their watch and check the time of the wounding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: On the day in question, what, exactly, were you wearing?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I had brown trousers and a yellow jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you possibly describe the shade of yellow that your jacket was?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I think it was lemony-yellow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Was your hair long or short at the time of the incident?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I had long hair, and that had been my style for quite a few years. During wartime, there was no hairdresser available for me to do my hair, so I had my hair very long.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And were you, on the day of the incident, wearing your hair tied up or was it down?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I had it down. I never tie it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, Ms. Dzevlan. Thank you for that. Mr. President, can I seek the admission of a couple of associated exhibits? There are, I believe, three exhibits which have not been admitted. They are 09603, 09949, and 40058P. I seek to tender them at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And 9536, Quick Time --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I believe that was recently admitted as P2207.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, they will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's give them numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. They will be Exhibit P2293 to P2295 respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Madam, you will be asked by Mr. Karadzic further questions. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Dzevlan.

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You knew immediately that you had been hit by a bullet from a rifle; right?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I didn't know immediately. I just felt the pain. But when I came to the hospital, they told me I had been hit by a bullet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Dzevlan, if you could put a pause between the question and answer, because both of your words should be interpreted into English and French. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us this: You were moving from the hospital towards your home when you were hit; right?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What were all the things you did on that day?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I just went to the hospital to get medicine, and nothing else. I went back.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D3234, could I have that in e-court, please, so that we try to mark a few locations that are important, as far as this incident is concerned. 1D3234.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You've lived in Dobrinja for a long time; right?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with the layout of these buildings?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't take my glasses. I cannot see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I offer you my own glasses?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You left your glasses at the waiting room; is that what you meant, Ms. Dzevlan? No problem, we'll take --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, may I ask you the following: Did you take the same route from home to hospital and from the hospital to your home?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you pass by any military facilities along the way?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: No. That's a civilian area in Dobrinja. To this day, I mean, it's only civilians who are living there, the general population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see. Did you pass by a street called Branilaca Dobrinja, the Defenders of Dobrinja nowadays?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I really don't know what the street names are in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can look at the city map and see what the former name was. Do you know that the command of the Dobrinja Brigade was on that street?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in Dobrinja, there was a brigade?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I just heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of Ismet Hadzic, its commander?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that it had between 4.500 and 6.000 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You certainly know why it was that the Serbs didn't take all of Dobrinja; right?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there fighting in and around Dobrinja often? I'm not talking about that day specifically.

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: There was a great deal of shelling. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This Muslim brigade, this Dobrinja Brigade, did it try to take Dobrinja IV?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please cast a glance at this, at this Google image, aerial image. Do you see the bridge where you were wounded? The street is Nikola Demonja.

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I think the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you wait a minute until assisted by our Usher. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. It's hard for me to find my way. Just a minute. This is the river, this is the bridge. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please put number 1 there?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And also if you could mark this more precisely; first of all, the arrow depicting the direction in which you were moving?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: As I was returning from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you were hit.

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you then mark -- could you then mark the next bridge -- or, rather, the next street where the separation line was? You know where the separation line was; right?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not at the separation line, but I do know -- I mean, later on after the war, I found out where the separation line was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark that for us?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: [Marks]. I assume that that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To this day, it belongs to Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These buildings to the right -- actually, could you put number 2 there by this line; that is, this street?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The building to the right, that was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: To the right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The buildings on the left were under whose control? Could you please put number 3 to the west of this street?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Under whose control were they?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: The Bosnian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you mark the building where you lived?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you mark the Dobrinja Hospital?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I think it was here. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see. Could you then mark the direction that you were moving in? Would you draw a line there?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I cannot really find my way. But if this is it, I was moving this way. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now please mark the church in Meljine [as interpreted]? Nice and slow, just take a look. The church in Veljine; right?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes, but I cannot really find my way here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you now mark the building from which you think the shot came, the one that wounded you, if it's not the church?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I can't do it this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You had been behind a shelter and you walked out. Did you hear bullets hitting the shelter?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How much time had elapsed from the moment you left the shelter until you were hit? Tell us either in terms of metres or in terms of time.

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't paying attention. I was on my bicycle, I was riding my bicycle. Was it half a minute or whatever, I really didn't have any feeling of that kind. Time was of no significance to us during the war, so I really cannot say. As soon as I left the shelter, I was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, you said at one point - I'll try to find it now - that you first heard shots and then you were hit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us have a look at the first statement. Do we need to mark anything else here? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know there where it says "Google," could you please put the date and could you sign it?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1048, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the statement of Ms. Dzevlan. D670 is what I have. It was recently admitted by the Prosecution. Can we see it, please, both in English and in Serbian. Oh, yes, yes. D670, that means it's already been admitted. Could we please have both the English and the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You first saw bullets flying around you, and then you were hit?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: No, no, I was hit first. I didn't even realise that I had been wounded until I saw these bullets ricochetting on the ground. Then I realised that I was being shot at, and I went on riding my bicycle. I assume that I would have been killed had I fallen off my bicycle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How do you know that these are ricochets? Are you knowledgeable about this kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm not knowledgeable about this kind of thing, but I have heard what a ricochet is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, what was the distance between and among these bullets? It was your assessment that it was automatic weapons; that's what you say in your statement?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: That's my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you went on riding your bicycle; right?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This shelter on the bridge, to the best of your knowledge, was used for what?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: So that civilians could safely cross from one part of Dobrinja to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And on the other side, was there a shelter on the other side as well? Were both sides of the bridge protected by barricades, both up-stream and down-stream?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The one on the other side, down-stream, it was protection from what?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the name is, but down there, that village. I mean, there were troops there, I mean Serb troops. They were firing too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was Nedzarici; right?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Oh, yes, Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Nedzarici is over 1.000 metres away from that bridge?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I'm not very knowledgeable about that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm a bit puzzled by the fact that you first said that you were hit at 1630 hours. Do you agree that had this statement remained as such, the visibility would have been assessed quite differently, because in Sarajevo, at 1630 in winter-time, it's rather dark, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Well, yes, quite. But I did say, when I made my statement, that I could not orient myself in time, because during the war, time didn't mean anything to us. Day-time and the dark, that was the only kind of time that we distinguished during the war; actual hours did not mean a thing. When I said "1630" at one point in time, it must have been just totally off the cuff. It was in the afternoon; it wasn't in the morning. It wasn't dark, because it was impossible for us civilians to move about in the dark in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to wait --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. I have an objection to the assertion by Dr. Karadzic that at 1630 it was rather dark in Sarajevo. That is not a matter in evidence. It's disputed by the Prosecution. We will accept that sunset was at 1624 and that twilight extended -- civil twilight was at 1655 and astronomical twilight was at 1806, but certainly we do not accept that it's an agreed fact that it was dark at 1630.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But is the accused not able to put his question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, he can, but he has -- he's assuming a matter not in evidence. He's assuming it's been proven that it was dark at 1630, and that has not been proven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But, Mr. Gaynor, didn't the witness agree with that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: With the suggestion that at 1630, it was dark?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Yes. She said: "Well, yes, quite, but I did say ..." and then she carried on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that the witness did say those words. I'm not sure that she was agreeing as to the precise level of darkness in Sarajevo at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But she said, "Well, yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. As Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When it's cloudy in the valley of Sarajevo, it's somewhat darker, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the time, on the actual hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First you said it was cloudy, and today, on page 9, you said that it was a bright day. Can you help us with this so that we definitely decide on what kind of a day it was?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Well, it was winter-time, it was cloudy, but there was visibility. I mean, there was light. I mean, what can I tell you about light? I don't understand what you're trying to ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the interpretation that we received here. It said "bright," and I think that that's exactly what you said. "Svetao," that kind of day, that means a clear day, a bright day?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Well, it was visible, because I was riding my bicycle, I left home after lunch, and I know that it was still day-time when I was admitted into hospital. The neighbours who were in front of the building, I mean, they wouldn't be standing outside. Nobody would be standing outside during the night. Nobody would be standing there in the dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, it remains that the day was a cloudy one; right?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have 65 ter 20571 for a moment, please. I believe that this has been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2292, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I would kindly ask the Court Clerk to switch on the pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please indicate the exact spot where you were hit, and put an X? Can you please zoom out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just wait.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you indicate the direction in which you were moving?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you were driving on the left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, can you place the number 1 there?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can you also put the number 2 next to the church tower, although it is visible?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This building that we see next to the number 2, can you mark it with the number 3, please?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who controlled that building, Ms. Dzevlan?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On which side of the street is it?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: What do you mean, on which side of the street?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it on this side of the separation line or from this side?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: It's from this side, from the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please put your signature and date?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have this admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Exhibit D1049.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 65 ter -- it's a still photo from footage, and I think the number is 20571, 65 ter. Can we then have 1D23 -- sorry, 3235, from 14 to 18:40.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we freeze the last frame, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is where you were shot, the place that you were showing to Mr. Hogan; right?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you describe your hair as long hair?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: This was my hair style after the war, and it's common knowledge that women often change their hair-do. As you can see, I have longer hair again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this still photo admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you produce one? Did you say "still photo" or this video?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe we can use this still photo. It's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless you produce a still photo from this, I don't think it's technically possible. Why don't you admit this video-clip, if it is not in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The video-clip has been admitted. It's one of the associated exhibits --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's another -- yes, thank you. Can we have that number? Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. It was 40058P. I don't have the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Exhibit P2295, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we don't know the time-frame for this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the time-frame. 18:14 to 18:40. So 18 minutes 14 seconds to 18 minutes 40 seconds --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- is what we have just seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Dzevlan, how many times were you shot?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I think twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. President, just to correct the record, Mr. Reid has just corrected me. The excerpts tendered by the Prosecution did not include this particular portion of the video, so it might be wise to give this particular portion a separate exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We admit this separately as a Defence exhibit, Exhibit D1050.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were hit with two bullets. Where did those bullets end?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were they extracted from your body?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: No, they penetrated through my body.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then in that case, we have four wounds, two entry wounds and two exit wounds; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were hit both on the left side and the right side?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we then say that it was the buttock muscle that you were hit in?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was any bone in your body damaged as a result?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did those bullets only scratch you or did they pass through the muscle tissue?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: They passed through the muscle tissue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So in such a condition with these two torn muscles, you continued riding your bicycle to your neighbour's house?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now have P1893 so that we can see what the medical doctors have to say about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at this diagnosis and the discharge form. "Vulnus transsclopetarium reg glutei bill," which means entry and exit wound of both gluteal region?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the doctors did not specify which wounds were entry wounds and which were exit wounds?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the doctors establish the point of entry and exit of both bullets?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I don't think that was that much relevant at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Ms. Dzevlan, being a doctor myself, I think it is important to indicate the entry and exit point of a bullet. How did it happen that you were hit in the left side as well? Where did that bullet come from?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Probably from the same place that the first one came.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were they horizontal or was one higher and the other lower? Do you have that information?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I don't know what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you were standing up, did one bullet enter at a higher level and the other at the lower level or were they in the same line?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I have a wound along the whole length. I don't know how they entered my body.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the bicycle seat also hit by the bullets?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So we can agree, can't we, that there is no indication here of the entry and exit points? This wound, was that a horizontal one or a slanted one?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: It was horizontal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your testimony today, you said that you think that the bullet was fired either from the church or from Dobrinja IV. What makes you say that?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I don't understand. This is where the Army of Republika Srpska was, and the barricades were erected precisely for the protection of the civilians. That's why we had those barriers, because there was sniping coming from the church and from Dobrinja IV.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is the criterion on the basis of which you claim that because Serbs were there, this is where the bullet came from; right?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I said that the bullet came from the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that, but can you tell me on the basis of what did you say that? What led you to say that it was either Dobrinja IV or the church?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I don't know where else it could have come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You don't think that there were troops and weapons and rifles in the Muslim part of Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: There were civilians living in that part of Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you consider a defence line also to be a civilian feature?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Between you and the Serbian position, was there a Muslim defence line?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the Muslims control the building that you marked, and that the Serbs could not capture it because it was defended?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Well, I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that it was a calm day and that a cease-fire was in force; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's what you heard on the radio; right?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there was fighting and that UNPROFOR was sending reports about fighting taking place all over the city?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 65 ter 09603.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for this, Ms. Dzevlan: Do you remember that during Bajram, people celebrate by firing from weapons?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did people shoot into the air during Bajram?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. But it is a custom to fire from fire-arms during holidays?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I don't know about other holidays, but I do know that there is no shooting on Bajram.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 3 of this document, which pertains to the 6th of January. Page 3, item 1, sub-items B and C. Well, there it is: "Unstable throughout the reporting period." And then it goes on to say that the BSA was shelling northern and western areas of the city: [In English] "Along with the city centre all week long. Most frequent BSA targets were Stup, Zuc ... " and so on. Now, look at C, where it says that the Bosnian side shelled, but I have to read it in English so that you can get a translation: [In English] "BiH shelling mainly confined to areas of Lukavica, Grbavica and BSA side of confrontation line in Vogosca ..." [Interpretation] Therefore, there was fighting all day long on that date.

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I don't know. All these places are so far from Dobrinja for me to know that. I know that there was no shooting in Dobrinja. I don't know about other parts of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is Lukavica far away, is Kula far away?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, one kilometre, two, three, four, as the crow flies. I don't know. At that time, I had no need to go to Lukavica. I had heard of it, but I had no need to go there. I did go to Luka [as interpreted], but it is also far away, since I lived in Dobrinja. When you stay in your flat, you stay indoors. You can't hear very well any distant shooting. You can only hear close fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that Lukavica and Kula are about 2.000 metres away and that the airport is about 1.000 metres away?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm not very familiar with these distances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in your statement -- actually, in the transcript that in the beginning of the war, the JNA was firing at the building that you were in from a tank and that the Patriotic League came to defend the area; right?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Serbs live in that building too?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a tank shell would have pierced the wall of such a building?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: It actually did in one apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know who commanded this tank brigade in Lukavica at the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I assume it was the Army of Republika Srpska. Actually, the army, the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the Yugoslav People's Army in the beginning of the war, Enver Hadzihasanovic was commander of that brigade when the war started. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Enver Hadzihasanovic, was he a Muslim, and was he later on a high-ranking officer of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Judging by his first and last names, would you infer that he was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is Vojnicko Polje far away from you?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How far?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: About a kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that on the 3rd of January, a Serb woman was killed there and other persons were wounded in Nedzarici; on the 3rd of January that year?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't manage to up-load this in e-court, so could we please have it placed on the ELMO, the English version, and then -- here it is. I'm going to read it out. Could you please lower it a bit. [In English] No, no, no, upper side. Thank you. [Interpretation] This is a report of "Srna" for foreign correspondents. It says: "Muslim snipers from Vojnicko Polje killed a woman, and wounded another person on Monday in Nedzarici (Western Sarajevo) ...," and so on and so forth. Had you heard of that, that this woman in your neighbourhood was killed three days before you were wounded.

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: No. That is very far away. There were barricades towards Vojnicko Polje. I had no way of knowing all this. We did not have all this information during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But did you watch TV, right, and you listened to the radio?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Well, we didn't have any electricity at the time. We had this small battery-operated radio, and from time to time we listened to the news.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this report be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Can we see another report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that it was peaceful during that days; right?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Well, I cannot remember right now on which days it was peaceful and which days it wasn't. But on that day, when I was supposed to go and get this medicine because, well, my mother was afraid, she feared for my life, and of course she was right. And I had to go and get that medicine. Now, I cannot say exactly which day and at what time there was no shooting and no shelling.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show on the ELMO again another document, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the 5th of January. I'm going to read it in English so that you can read an interpretation: [In English] "Last night, on the Sarajevo front passed with occasional Muslim small-arms provocations against Serb position on the Jewish cemetery (Sarajevo centre) and upon Serb communities of Grbavica (Sarajevo centre) and Dobrinja IV (Serb Sarajevo). Wednesday morning on the front saw usual Muslim sniper activity. "The Christmas cease-fire on the RS northern frontiers ...," and so on. [Interpretation] Did you hear that on the radio, that I had declared a unilateral Christmas cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what did you hear on the radio; that there was some kind of cease-fire on?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Well, probably. I can no longer remember. It's been a long time. I just know that during those few hours when I was supposed to go and get that medicine and come back, it was peaceful. Now, was it peaceful the entire day, in the morning as well?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe that you're not going to admit this either, so then let's put another report there on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to note, in passing, that none of these three reports have been provided to the Prosecution by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I hear the explanation as to this, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we've just received them, Excellency, and I didn't have enough time -- I mean, we didn't have enough time to up-load them in e-court. We're certainly going to do that. Since you are not admitting them, I'm just using them to refresh the witness's memory, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, it's the 6th of January, it's the day when you were wounded --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not an appropriate explanation. That being the case, you are obliged to disclose this material to the Prosecution. And having said that, let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do ask for an apology. This happens rarely. But we received this only this morning, and that's why we didn't have enough time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read the first paragraph -- or, actually, I'm not going to read the first paragraph, but then -- actually, was it Thursday when you were wounded?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I don't know what day it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what it says: [In English] "Muslim forces renewed on Thursday morning at 6.45 a.m., an artillery infantry attack started on Wednesday upon Sarajevo, Serb communities Grbavica and Raca, reported the Informative Service of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps in Lukavica. Three persons were killed ...," and so on and so on. [Interpretation] So on that day, there was considerable activity. You didn't know about that; right?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us have a look at the 7th, just another piece of information, what was going on at Dobrinja IV, and then we're going to leave this particular topic. Do you remember, Ms. Dzevlan, that I declared cease-fires both for Muslim and Christian holidays and that I asked that no fire be opened either on Muslim or Christian holidays?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember. I had greater concerns than that. I cannot really remember that. I had a young child. I had to provide food, water. I had old parents. I really don't remember that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at this "Thursday." Was Friday the 7th of January, 1994? And on the previous day, on Thursday, it was the 6th: [In English] "On Thursday, at approximately 1000 hours, Muslim artillery and infantry attempted to penetrate Serb territory in Dobrinja [B/C/S spoken]." It's the Dobrinja IV that you've been talking about; right?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know from your Serb neighbours what holidays are on the 6th and 7th of January?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: At that time, I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the 6th of January is Christmas Eve, and that the 7th of January is Christmas Day?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: I agree, but it is irrelevant to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Dzevlan, for having come to testify. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just one question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, do you know the precise time of sunset on the 6th of January, 1994?

utterances.speaker: SANIJA DZEVLAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And if I were to put it to you that it was at 1624, do you have any comment to make about that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. It was cloudy. This is speculation, truly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Mr. Gaynor asked the witness whether she knew. But if parties agree on the sunset, then there's no need to put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. I'd invite the Defence to agree on that. I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you agree, Mr. Karadzic, that sunset time on that day was 1624?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's plausible. But since it was cloudy, it cannot be determined. We can only receive information from some astronomical institute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's a separate matter whether it was cloudy or not, but whether you can agree on the time of sunset on that date. Ms. Dzevlan, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Tribunal and the Bench, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague. Now you are free to go. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break, about one hour, and we'll resume at half past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Glavas. If you could kindly take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Glavas, could you please tell us your full name?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Tihomir Glavas.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Glavas, on 30 March 2009, did you testify before the State Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a Defence witness in the case of Rade Veselinovic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you, since that occasion, reviewed the transcript of your testimony during those proceedings?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And on February 3rd and 4th of this year, 2011, did you meet with members of the Office of the Prosecutor, including me, to give a statement on some additional matters relating to your observations and experiences during the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was that statement read back to you in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, in The Hague and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters didn't hear the first part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think I can safely move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And then yesterday, did you again meet with me and other members of the OTP to review and sign a further statement consolidating the evidence from your testimony and your statement of February 3rd and 4th?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in that further statement you signed yesterday, you made some small corrections and clarifications to parts of your 4 February statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, other than those, if I asked you the same questions yet again that gave rise to that written evidence, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Absolutely the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then, Your Honours, could I ask that the amalgamated statement, which was signed yesterday, 65 ter 90223, be the next Prosecution exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2296, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll now read a summary of this witness's written evidence. A career police officer, this witness held the post of commander of the Public Security Station, or SJB, in Hadzici in the period leading up to the outbreak of war. From April until August 1992, he served as chief of the Public Security Station for the Serbian municipality of Hadzici. In August of that year, he was transferred to Ilidza, where he took up the post of deputy chief of the SJB for the Serbian municipality of Ilidza. In his capacity as chief of the SJB, the witness was a member of the Crisis Staff for the Serbian municipality of Hadzici. The Crisis Staff was the highest organ of authority in Hadzici municipality. The witness recounts an incident where, on 20 May 1992, during the course of a police operation to search for weapons, three men, civilians from the settlement of Musici, were killed. The decision to carry out this operation to recover weapons emanated from the Crisis Staff. Men from the settlement were arrested and detained in the local sports and recreation centre. Additionally, it was the Crisis Staff's decision that men of military age from other settlements in the area should be arrested and detained. Some women and children were also detained, but not as a rule. The decision as to the establishment of a detention facility within the sports centre was made by the Crisis Staff. It was also their decision that it should be guarded by the Territorial Defence. The intention was that detainees should be kept for exchange. In June 1992, the majority of the detainees were transferred to Kula Prison. On one occasion, the witness learned that paramilitaries had entered the sports centre and abused the detainees. They attempted to do the same thing at the garage under the municipality building, where Bosniaks were also held. The witness confronted the members of this paramilitary group, who withdrew. The witness also gives evidence of the presence and operation of Seseljevci and other paramilitary units in the Ilidza municipality, and the combined efforts of the police and military to remove these units because of their criminal behaviour. That's the summary of his written evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Glavas, I'd like to ask you some questions based on some of this written evidence, but, first of all: Do you recall, during our meeting yesterday, reviewing some additional photos and documentation?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in your amalgamated statement, your written evidence, at paragraph 6 you talked about the founding session of the Serbian municipality of Hadzici in the first part of April 1992. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 01503, minutes of a meeting dated 11 April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Glavas, is this one of the documents you saw yesterday?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see your name at number 19, on the bottom right-hand corner of this document, as a member of the advisory organ --

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- of Hadzici Serb municipality?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I see my name.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document relates to?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I think that this is a sort of -- I would call it a working body, since you had already said that I had stated that on that date, the so-called All Serbian Assembly or rally was held, which involved all the Serb residents of Hadzici. And at this Assembly, the Serbian municipality of Hadzici was constituted. Certain legitimate authority organs were elected on that occasion, and the list shown here, I think, contains the name of the people who were members of this so-called working body. And I can tell you that on that occasion, in addition to the decision to set up the Serbian municipality of Hadzici, other organs of authority were elected, such as the president of the municipality and the chairman of the Executive Board, and I think that the Assembly at the same time endorsed my appointment to the position of the chief of the police station or the SJB Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could this be a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P2297, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Glavas, do you recall the function of this working body? What did it do?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Well, their function was similar to any other body, so somebody had to preside over this assembly, and they chaired over this meeting as a sort of working body.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where were the municipality offices located?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: In the municipal building, which is in down-town Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in answering that question, are you referring to the offices of the Assembly of the Serbian Municipality of Hadzici or pre-war?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: No. No, that's not what I meant. If we're still talking about the All-Serbian Assembly, then the premises were in -- on the ground floor of the sports centre in Hadzici where this meeting took place, not in the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did they remain in that location?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did they remain in that location throughout your time working in Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did they remain in that location between April and August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just relating to premises: In your written evidence, at paragraph 7, you refer to the establishment of the police force and indicate that you went to some provisional premises in the cultural centre. And in that regard, I'd like to look at 65 ter 01439. Now, Mr. Glavas, do you recognise the image on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, only you did not put your question correctly. You said "cultural centre." That was the workers' club that was owned by the former maintenance and repair centre of Hadzici. So it's on the right-hand side of the picture, this building here [indicates]. This is the building where the -- where the Security Centre was. Do I need to do it now again?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, I think that's fine. Thank you. If this could be a Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2298, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did the police forces remain in this location between April and August of 1992 or did they relocate during this period?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: No, they did not remain until August. They stayed there for a while. I cannot remember exactly when was it that we moved to other premises in Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What other premises did you move to?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: This was mainly the ground floor in the municipal building of Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move on to another area relating to your testimony in the Veselinovic case, and that's the Crisis Staff. You discussed the Crisis Staff in a number of areas, and in the Veselinovic case you describe the Crisis Staff as the highest organ of authority in the Hadzici municipality. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What did you understand, then, to be its competencies or its authority? What's the basis of your answer in that regard?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Well, under such circumstances during wartime or during an immediate threat of war, a crisis staff is formed, and it has all the powers relating to civilian police and other affairs. So, practically, they assumed the role of both the executive and legislative organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall when the Crisis Staff in Hadzici municipality was formed?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: In April of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who were its members?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Members of the staff were people who were elected to certain positions, such as the president of the municipality, the chairman of the Executive Board, the representative of the police, which was yours truly because I was the chief of police at the time, there was a military representative as well, and in this particular case such as Hadzici, we had representatives of the management of the military facility, which is maintenance and repair centre, because that institution played a significant role before the war and also during the war. For that reason, their presence on the Crisis Staff was required as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was there -- how was it -- how was it established? Was there an initiative that you recall?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I think that it happened immediately after the All-Serbian Assembly that I mentioned earlier and as a result of the overall complex security and political situation in the area. It was a well-known fact that co-operation between representatives of the Serbian-Bosniak authorities was not very good, so the Serbian people stated at the Assembly that they should organise themselves, and which was followed by the initiative to set up the Crisis Staff by the people who I mentioned in my previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did it have any premises that it kept to itself? Where was it located?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. In the municipal building, there was a conference room where we met on most occasions and took decisions related to certain situations in the municipality of Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How often did it meet?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Well, you know, every morning, a meeting would be held, but I wouldn't call these official meetings. This was, more or less, briefing sessions. People who were in charge of certain areas would provide feedback information to the Crisis Staff. However, if there was a need prompted by the information gathered on the ground, then we would meet officially. So, basically, we met every day, but the decisions that were relevant for the military and civilian, or other affairs, we would discuss such decisions before taking them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you attend these meetings?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've just said that the meetings were daily. Did you attend every day?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: No, I did not attend every day, because at the time I had a commander of the police station who, by virtue of his position, could replace me. So, actually, the commander was the one who went to most meetings, but I am not exonerating myself from whatever was said at the Crisis Staff. And there was a way for me to find out what was being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: When I was at the SJB while he attended the Crisis Staff meetings, he would come back and he would regularly inform me about the topics that were discussed on the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what was his name?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: His name was Brane Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What about the decision-making process? Did the Crisis Staff require your presence, as police chief, to take decisions?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Of course, but I said that the commander could stand in by virtue of his position. So it was irrelevant who of the two of us would attend. However, the decisions by the Crisis Staff were taken through the following procedure: We would obtain certain information of interest for the Security Service as well as intelligence that was of interest for the military, and depending on the content of this information, if it affected public security, which means domestic issues and the rear of the territory, this decision was usually taken by the police chief's station, that is, me, whereas all the other military aspects were taken care of by the army. The decisions were taken and would be given to me at the Crisis Staff meeting. In my testimony in the Veselinovic case, I outlined the organisational structure of the SJB, which consisted of a number of organisational units, and one of the most important ones was the police station that had a crime prevention and investigation unit. As the chief, based on the decision I received, I decided which of my employees would implement this decision. If it had to do with crime, I would give it to that particular unit. If it had to do something with regular police work, I would put my initials on the decision and pass it on to either the commander or any other head of any other organisational unit. So that was the organisational structure, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What form were these decisions -- Crisis Staff decisions made in? Were they in writing or were they orally? How were they communicated?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: For the most part, they were in writing, because the Crisis Staff was in a position to make very important decisions at the time. You know what the situation was. It was very complex, from the point of view of the safety and security of citizens. So, in principle, such decisions were made in writing, and they were submitted in the way that I've already described.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to talk now about the implementation of some of these decisions and refer to parts of your written evidence in that regard. For example, at paragraph 26 of your written evidence, you said that you didn't know for a fact who made the order to collect military-aged Bosniaks in the sports hall, but you assume, like other decisions, it came from the Crisis Staff, as no other body had the authority to make that decision. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: That's right, I do remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So who implemented this decision, then? Who carried out this decision?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: If you are referring specifically to taking people into detention, it was done by the regular police and Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, also in your written evidence, you said that it was the Crisis Staff's decision that the detention facility at the sports centre should be under the military or the Territorial Defence. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I do, and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So was that, then, the case? Did the military or the Territorial Defence control the sports centre?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
