utterances.text: Yes. I'll try to explain certain things as briefly as possible now. For certain reasons for which citizens were being taken in, primarily citizens of Bosnian ethnicity, was the reason that we had reliable information to the effect that they had long rifles. First, these people would be interviewed by the Crime Prevention Service. After these interviews, these persons would be transferred to the cultural and sports centre. From this point of view, I really cannot explain why it was under the military, the cultural and sports centre, but I'm going to tell you what I've already said to you in Sarajevo. I remember exactly the names and surnames of the people who were guarding this sports facility, and I remember Trifko Ignjatovic; Milovic, Rade; Milovic, Momo; Duka, Radovan; and others. All of them were members of the Territorial Defence, and I claim that in this way, the sports centre was practically never under the Security Service or, rather, the station that I was at the time, at least for as long as I was in Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: These people you just named, do you recall who they were subordinate to? Who was their commander at that time?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Someone from these formations, but I don't know the exact name or surname.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your written evidence, you also said that on 22 June 1992, the majority of detainees at the sports centre were transferred to Kula, and you thought that this was on the order of the Crisis Staff. And I'd like to know on what basis you think that.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Well, because I was aware that decisions at the level of the municipality of Hadzici, including such a decision, could -- couldn't have been made by anyone but the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you know how the prisoners were moved?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, and I'll explain why. It just so happened that sometime from the 18th until the 20 something of June, I was away. I went to visit my family in Serbia. And when I contacted my commander by telephone, of course, I asked him what was going on at the station that he and I headed together, and he told me, inter alia, that the entire Bosniak population that had been detained at the sports centre was transferred to Kula. To tell you the truth, my reaction was that I was not in favour of that kind of thing. Quite simply, I knew that if these people left, if they were no longer under the Serb authorities in Hadzici, then somebody else will be deciding on their exchange. And that is basically what happened. Some of these people were exchanged, but that was not the situation in each and every case. They were exchanged for the Serb population that was detained in Tarcin or, rather, the silo. After that, we had some terrible problems. We were under enormous pressure by citizens of Serb ethnicity who were aware at the time that they would be in a very, very difficult position, that it would be very hard for them to get their own people out of the silo and the elementary school in Pazaric. That is where they were detained. And, indeed, it was very hard to get people out of these collection centres where they were detained.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you were briefed by your commander as to what happened, did he tell you -- when you were briefed by your commander about the transfer, did he tell you who had authorised the transfer?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I remember that I asked him specifically who gave this order, and he said, Ratko Radic, commander of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you say the majority of the people in the sports centre were transferred, in fact, you just said the entire population that had been detained in the sports centre was transferred, do you have any idea what number of people that represents? How many were transferred to Kula?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure. I think it may be between 180 and 200 persons. I'm not sure of that particular bit of information, that it is unequivocally correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to move on, but still on the theme of the decision-making or the implementation of decisions: You described, at length in your testimony in the Veselinovic case, the operation by police forces in Musici settlement for the seizure of weapons, and I'd like to know under whose decision that operation was carried out.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Absolutely, it was the decision of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And how do you know?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, I know what the practice was at the time. I, as the chief of the station at the time, I quite simply could not have -- although I had certain knowledge, I could not have organised any action that was of interest from the point of view of the service I headed if I did not have an appropriate decision of the Crisis Staff. That is one thing. And, secondly, the situation was very difficult at the time, it was a time of great uncertainty, and people were very reluctant to take upon any kind of responsibility. At the time, as a person, on a personal level, I wanted to have it black on white, as our people say. I wanted to have a decision in writing before I went out and did anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, finally, in paragraph 41 of your written evidence, still relating to the incident at Musici, you said that you were informed that the weapons seized during the course of that operation were divided, on the decision of the Crisis Staff, and redistributed to members of the police or the military. How do you know that this was done on the basis of a decision by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: We couldn't have done it just like that. It had to be a decision of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move on now to a couple more photographs, the first being 65 ter 01436.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Glavas, did you see this photograph yesterday in preparation for your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I do. I don't know if you can see it here on your monitors, but this is the sports centre [indicates], and on the left we see the elementary school in Hadzici [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is it similar to how it appeared, to your recollection, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I think so. I think that's about it. That's what the sports centre looked like.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could that be the next Prosecution exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2299, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, could we move on to 65 ter 01437, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Glavas, did you see this photograph in preparation for your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What does it represent, then? Do you recognise what's depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I said yesterday that this is roughly the left wing of the municipality building. What you see down there are the garages. Sorry, this is what I meant [indicates]. That's the garages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The witness is indicating, with the cursor, the three doors at the bottom of the photograph when he describes the garages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Glavas, you've said this is the left wing of the municipality building, and I'm wondering if you could tell us where, in this building, the conference room that you described earlier is located.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I can't. I cannot orient myself on the basis of this photograph. Do you think you could zoom out a bit, and then if I see the entire building --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could have this marked as a Prosecution exhibit, we could go, probably, to a better photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2300, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we try 65 ter 01438, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Glavas, do you recognise what's depicted on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the municipality building, and this part here [indicates] is what I saw on the first photograph. This was the main part [indicates], and this is where the entrance was. And the hall that we talked about a few minutes ago should have been somewhere around here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If I could just get you to slow up for a minute. When the witness indicated the main part, he pointed, with the cursor, to an entryway above a white car that was shown in the photo. And I didn't see, Mr. Glavas, where you went with the cursor when you mentioned the hall we talked about a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I've already said that it should be somewhere around here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Indicating a set of three windows on the second floor above the garages on the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, while we have this photo on the screen in front of us: You mentioned also that eventually the police services were relocated to the ground floor of the municipality building. And where, please, were the police services located? Could you show us on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: That's right. I indicated a moment ago that this was the entrance [indicates]. And this on the left here, these two windows, that's where our duty offices were [indicates], if I can put it that way. That's where our duty police officer was, the one who checked people coming in and out of the building. You cannot see the rest of the ground floor of this building where our offices were. We did not have very many offices, but they were basically there on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wonder, would it help Your Honours, for the witness to circle these locations so we could be abundantly clear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And perhaps he could have some help.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, then, Mr. Glavas, could you mark, with a circle and a number 1, the location of your police services and the duty officer's post that you've just indicated?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Well, I don't know if it's necessary for me to mark this. Well, let it be number 1 [marks]. So this is the entrance to the building. Then the window here on the left-hand side, number 2 [marks], that was the window of the room that was relatively small, and basically that was the room where our duty police officers were who were checking people coming in and out of the building. And now number 3 [marks], you cannot see the interior, but basically on the ground floor, that is where the offices of the Public Security Station of Hadzici were.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And can you mark with the number 4 the location of the conference room where you recall the Crisis Staff holding their meetings?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: [Marks]. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, does this building resemble -- to the best of your recollection, does this building on the photograph appear as it was in 1992?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I believe you said, No, rather than, Yes. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I said that this is not what it looked like in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what's different?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't devastated, which is what it looks like now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Other than the damage that you've seen, are -- no, I think that's fine. Could that be the next Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are admitting it: Mr. Glavas, could you kindly put the date and your signature on this picture, on the right bottom? Today is the 14th of February, 2011.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2301, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we remove that from the screen, just one more question about these garages, Mr. Glavas.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In your written evidence, at paragraphs 53 and 54, you referred to people of Bosniak ethnicity being held in the garage below the municipality building. Does this photograph depict the garage that you refer to?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You would like to mark that garage on the previous photo? Yes. Why don't you up-load P2301.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps you can mark that garage with the number 5.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: [Marks]. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, can that still be P2301?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be kept as it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Glavas, how many people were held in this garage at the time you referred to?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I think that it would be about 30 people. I have to say that as for the people who were in this garage, if you remember, I mentioned persons of Bosnian ethnicity who were brought in and interviewed. It's that category of people who had been interviewed. People like that were detained in these garages - how should I put this? - because it was nearby. Our premises were in the municipality building. Then after the interviews, such persons would be transferred to the sports centre, and practically, then, they would be kept there by the Territorial Defence or, later on, the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you know where these 30 people came from?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I think that it was mostly people from Muslic and Visasoci [phoen], and then some from Binjezevo [Realtime transcript read in error "Bicevo"] and some from Kuciste. That's a hamlet near Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On the transcript, it says "Bicevo." Do you mean Bicevo or do you mean Binjezevo?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Binjezevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just to move on to another area: In paragraph 19 of your written evidence, you referred to your conflicts with the political leadership in Hadzici and, to a certain extent, the military, saying that the political leadership didn't want to follow correct police procedures at that time. And you also mentioned something similar during your testimony in the Veselinovic case, which appears at paragraph 20 of your written evidence. You said you had certain disagreements with the people who governed the politics of both the police and army personnel back then. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who do you mean to refer to when you refer to these people?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I was primarily referring to the political leadership, headed by Mr. Ratko Radic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What was the nature of your disagreements?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Well, when I testified in the Veselinovic case, I said that I am your classical professional; that is to say, that I completed the regular School For the Interior, in the meantime I studied part-time while working, and I learned everything I knew in that area in that way. Everything I did on the basis -- I did on the basis of rules and regulations. However, that met with resistance, and some people at the time were calling me names. They said I was a formalist. You know, these were very complex times, very complex, from the point of view of security and politics in that area. They thought that certain things had to be done in haste. However, people were well aware that I spent a lot of time out in the field with my policemen, because, as I said, the situation was extremely difficult. We spent a lot of time at the defence lines initially. We did that more than our regular police work. I would stay out until 2.00 or 3.00 or 4.00 at night, and I mainly went to spend the night at my aunt's place because I didn't dare go to my own apartment in Hadzici. At the beginning of the war, they opened fire at my apartment, so I didn't really want to go there. They criticised me, why I did not go to Crisis Staff meeting, and practically at the time these Crisis Staff meetings boiled down to some formalities, if I can put it that way, and that is basically why I clashed with them. I simply thought that there was no need for me to attend every day, especially because I spent a lot of time on the ground with the police. At the time, my position, and I must say of all the police and part of the military, was that the priority was to defend the area of Hadzici and preserve it. How can I attend Crisis Staff meetings if we lose our positions in the field? There was ongoing activity, day in, day out, and we were under threat. We almost lost our positions. And that is why I clashed with them. So I worked out a compromise with Mr. Kovac. I agreed to leave. And, as I've already said, sometime around the 6th of August, I went to Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I realise we were sitting on a bit of a different schedule today, but I was just looking at the time and I wondered -- I hadn't heard Your Honours say anything about when we might break, and I thought I might raise it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was waiting for a go from the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a 20-minute break at 10 to 1.00. That means we will have two 80-minute sessions. Thank you. Let's go on until 10 to.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Certainly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You talked about Mr. Radic a few minutes ago, and I'd like to ask you a few questions about him now. In his capacity as Crisis Staff head and head of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza, was he subordinate to any organ or individual?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did Mr. Radic, in his function, have someone that he needed to report to?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I think that the Crisis Staff in every municipality, including Hadzici, acted independently, and I said earlier that it was authorised to take all the decisions relating to the area of their responsibility, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In the course of -- did Mr. Radic have any contact, to your knowledge, with any members of the Bosnian Serb political leadership?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With anyone in particular?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Well, he often told us that he met President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did he say why?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I cannot remember at the moment. But, on the other hand, I clearly remember that if it was necessary for him to put some of his ideas into practice, he would often refer to Dr. Karadzic and claim that he had agreed with him on certain things. After a while, I gained an expression [as interpreted] that he was misinforming us or, rather, abusing his contacts with Dr. Karadzic. However, due to the fact that he was so keen to implement his ideas, he would say that he had discussed and agreed to those things with Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you say he was misinforming you, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if you recall, in my statement that I gave in Sarajevo, I think that I mentioned a rather unpopular expression attached to the president of the municipality. I called him a person who was prone to manipulations. So I think that he was capable of presenting the situation in Hadzici to Mr. Karadzic in such a way that was untruthful. He would say one thing to us, and he would be doing something completely different.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you give us an example?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: An example of what?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've just said you think he was capable of presenting the situation in Hadzici to Mr. Karadzic in such a way that was untruthful. He would say one thing, and he would be doing something completely different. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I think that in one of my statements, I said, inter alia, that he would portray one situation to us, believing that we would receive assistance from outside, but then the next moment, when the situation was at its worst in Hadzici, when everything was on fire, Mr. Ratko Radic was nowhere to be seen, he was absent from this area. And I'm telling you the truth, and the entire public shares this opinion with me, the public of Hadzici. He was away, either with his family in Belgrade or at Pale, as he later said.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you indicated that you moved to Ilidza in August of 1992. Did you hold a similar position in the Crisis Staff, when you transferred to Ilidza, to the one you had occupied in Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who was a member of the Crisis Staff in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: It also involved functions; only different people were involved. The president of the Crisis Staff was a man whose name I cannot remember. There was a man called Lalovic, who was the chairman of the Executive Board. There was a representative of the police and a representative of the military as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who was the municipality head in Ilidza at the time you served there?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Nedjeljko Prstojevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did he occupy a function on the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I said he was the Crisis Staff commander or Crisis Staff president.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. The transcript, Mr. Glavas, read: "The president of the crisis staff was a man whose name I could not remember." That's why I asked you that question. Did you attend meetings of this Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Are you referring to the Ilidza Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Very seldom, and I will try and explain why. I came there in August, and up until October, to be precise, by the 21st of October, 1991, I did not discharge the duties of the chief. Consequently, I was not a member of the Crisis Staff. At the time, I was the assistant chief rather than the deputy chief. On the 21st, I was appointed chief of the station, and I have to say that at that time already, we very seldom attended Crisis Staff meetings for a simple reason: that at the time, we were already organised in such a way that we were more connected with the Ministry of the Interior, which involved receiving instructions and orders from them rather than from the local level.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where was the Crisis Staff in Ilidza located?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: It was a separate room for meetings in the municipal building, and that is where the meetings were held.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And how often did they meet?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you now. I know that initially there were much more meetings in Hadzici. I cannot remember clearly. I think I attended a couple of meetings in Ilidza only, because at that time certain things started to fall into place with respect to politics, army and police. A sort of rule of law started to be introduced. So we, as members of the Public Security Department, who were in charge of maintaining public law and order, did not have any particular need to meet quite often with the municipal authorities. Moreover, the Security Department was structured in such a way that we had stronger ties with the minister of the interior than with the local communities. The leaderships of local communities could only give an opinion or a suggestion, for example, concerning my appointment. However, the minister of the interior was not obliged to take that opinion into account, and it was up to him to appoint the chief of police as his discretionary right. As members of the Security Department, our duty was to keep the local authorities abreast of the things that were security-related, but only in the area that we covered.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in your written evidence, at paragraph 69, you describe your relationship with Mr. Prstojevic, and you noted that he was quite arrogant, and you had an argument on the phone with him and told him that you were responsible for security in Ilidza and he was in charge of politics, and that after that conversation, Prstojevic started asking you advice, rather than giving you orders. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You said he asked you if you could send police officers for this and that, but before, he used to order you to do this; not only to send police to military operations being conducted, but trying to assign police officers in the military for his own uses?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was that not a function, though, of his position as head of the Crisis Staff, as you've described him?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Well, yes, that was his position, but I am talking about the initial period when the service was organised in a different way, as opposed to the one that I just described. We were more and more in the position that when it involves affairs relating to public security, we would follow the instructions of our management from the Ministry of the Interior. So, practically, I was not duty-bound, even under the law, to inform him about certain things, with the exception of the things that explicitly related to the municipality of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just one more point of clarification. Where you said you're talking about the initial period when the service was organised in a different way, how was it organised, how was it different?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: What I meant was that there was no link between the top leadership in the Ministry of the Interior and the grassroot level, such as police station, in Hadzici and elsewhere. So under such circumstances, both the citizens and the leadership, and we, as well, thought that we were left to our own devices entirely, and we had, by the nature of things, to deal more with the Crisis Staff during that period than was the situation at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that covers the 20 minutes that you had indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have a break for 20 minutes and resume at 1.10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Glavas, before we move on, I'd actually like just to go back to the discussion that we were having about the transfer of prisoners from the sports centre to Kula on June 22nd. Now, that journey from Hadzici to Kula would have been a journey of many kilometres; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that journey crossed the boundaries of more than one municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'm willing to bet it would have involved crossing any number of check-points as well. Correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So what I'd like to know, given all that, is: What level of co-ordination between what organs and authorities would have been required for the detainees to make that journey?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: There could be co-ordination at the level of the municipalities between which the transport of these detainees took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would the military authorities not have been involved, given that check-points would have had to have been crossed?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Of course. That that was mainly done by the military authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So what organs would have involved in ensuring that journey came to an end? What organs would have been involved to make sure that journey took place as planned?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: The situation was such that due to some other reasons and security-related issues, and the ties between the area in the Serbian Sarajevo, presidents of the municipalities, who at the time were actually presidents of Crisis Staff, communicated very frequently in order to carry out certain operations. I assume that on this occasion, too, an agreement was reached between the competent presidents of the crisis staffs, which finally led to the transportation of these detainees. But please bear in mind that I'm giving you general descriptions. I said before that I was not there when these detainees were transferred to Kula, and I kindly ask you to take this into account.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move on to one final area, and it's a decision about paramilitaries in Ilidza, which begins at paragraph 71 of your written evidence. First, to your knowledge, was Mr. Prstojevic aware of the presence of paramilitaries in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I know that he knew about the existence of those paramilitary formations. When I moved to Ilidza, the commander of the police station, Vlatko Knezevic, was on extremely good terms with Mr. Prstojevic, and I received a lot of information from him. That's how I know that he knew about the paramilitary. But that was common knowledge at the time. It was no secret that there were paramilitary groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you also said that with respect to the unit of Branislav Gavrilovic, that they fought at the airport settlement, Doglodi and Otes. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you date, approximately, these operations at the airport settlement, Doglodi and Otes?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Doglodi and Otes could have happened sometime in August of 1992. I remember that because that was about the time when I went to Ilidza, when this action was carried out, so that would be approximately the month and the year.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could the operation in Otes you're referring to have taken place as late as December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: It is possible, it is possible, but I do know and I am personally familiar with that action because I was in Ilidza at the time. As I said, I was there from the 6th of August until I was appointed chief in October, so it's possible that this action took place in the month that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How did you know that they took part in these operations? And I notice you haven't given us a date for the airport settlement.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: The operation of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please start the answer from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Glavas, the interpreters couldn't hear you, so could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do so. So the operation relating to the airport settlement would -- definitely took place before the operation in Otes, and I remember that because at the time when the airport settlement operation was in progress, Mr. Tomislav Kovac was in Ilidza, and I succeeded him, and that's the reason why I know that this operation took place earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In your written evidence, you said that this unit had private political connections to go into these areas, that they were not on police or military orders. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: What I wanted to say was that the manner in which paramilitary formations could have come to a certain area, including the area of Hadzici, was such that it was based on friendship and other forms of relationships, so there was no need for any subordination or co-operation with state leaderships or organs. So that is the way in which certain paramilitary formations were brought to certain municipalities, based on friendship.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When we talk about the airport settlement, Doglodi and Otes, would you agree with me that those were front-line operations?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I didn't understand completely. What did you ask me about the actions?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The airport settlement, Doglodi and Otes were combat operations on the front-line, were they not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What kind of political connections would have -- would these units have had to go into these areas, areas of military control?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: They didn't need to have any other ties or relations, other than those based on personal friendships, for them to come to a certain area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What municipal area or what municipality were Doglodi and Otes found in?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: It's in the area of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you infer anything about the personal friendships or political connections, then, that they would have had to go into these combat areas?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, it was possible, based on personal connections. In one of my introductory notes either here or in Sarajevo, I describe the general situation in which it was considered that those people were welcomed under the circumstances. However, very soon we realised that we don't have much use of these men, so as the service and as the political leadership, we came into conflict with these formations due to some of their activities. And as I said before, they practically never wanted to go to separation lines that were located in forests or places like that. They preferred to go to residential areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, in your written evidence, at paragraph 74 of your amalgamated statement, you said the reason they went into those areas was so that they could steal and loot, and you referred specifically to Otes, Doglodi and the airport settlement. So how do you know that they were stealing and looting in those areas?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we know that because at the time it was a generally-known thing. At the time, it was a show of force on their part. We had terrible problems. We, as the Security Service, objectively speaking, could not oppose them because they threatened us with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What happened to the loot that they acquired?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it was basically used for their own purposes. It wasn't a political thing, it wasn't defined in any way. They had these private laws of their own; relationships, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll just -- I'd like to move to one final document, 65 ter 11576, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Glavas, in your written evidence you commented extensively on the local group of Seseljevci, led by Branislav Gavrilovic, and the document I'd like to show you now is a letter of approval, dated 9 July 1992, signed by Mr. Prstojevic, allowing Gavrilovic to use the motel facility in Gladno Polje and deserted summer houses in the vicinity for the needs of Serbian volunteer units from the front-lines of the Ilidza MUP.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've already referred in your written evidence to Gavrilovic being headquartered in the Vila Vocnjak in an orchard towards Rakovica. Is this the same -- does this document describe the same location?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Gladno Polje is a settlement in the area of Rakovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And can you explain to us or interpret the reference in this document to the Serbian volunteer units being from the lines of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza MUP?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I think that I told you yesterday what my comment would be in relation to this document. I'm not contesting its authenticity. I see the name and surname, "Nedeljko Prstojevic," I even see that it's his signature. However, I will never understand the content of this document, because I know with certainty that the ministry never had any paramilitary formations within their establishment. And the date here is the 9th of July, 1992; that is to say, it's the time before I arrived in Ilidza. Perhaps a better explanation would be provided by Mr. Tomislav Kovac, the then chief of police in Ilidza. I really do not know how -- actually, I'm telling you, I'm not contesting the authenticity of the text, of the signature, of the name. But, indeed, I find the content of the document quite unclear.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, given the witness's comments with respect to the authenticity of the document, and his confirmation that the location of the headquarters approved for Mr. Gavrilovic corresponds with what he had reported in his written evidence, I'd ask that this be the next Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2302, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That concludes the examination-in-chief, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we deal with associated exhibits? So you will be tendering all of them?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Not quite, Your Honours. The ones I -- of course, the ones that have already been admitted, we're not, but I've indicated a number of -- with some comments in this notification, that there are a number of documents we're not seeking to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I have the recent notification, so could you name the 65 ter numbers you are tendering?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections? They will all be admitted and given a number in due course. Yes, we have about an hour. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Just before you start: Tomorrow morning, we'll begin with another witness, won't we?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wasn't sure exactly how the timing was going to work, Your Honour, but you're right, there is another witness scheduled for tomorrow who, I think, given the allotted time, wouldn't consume the entirety of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to all. Good afternoon, Mr. Glavas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for having met up with my advisers and with myself briefly. Had we had more time, I'm sure we would have clarified some of the things that remain unclear so that we could move on faster.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I looked at your amalgamated statement only this morning. However, I shall try to put as many questions as possible that require only yes-or-no answers. Do we agree that you were a policeman during the days of the socialist system as well?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that even in the socialist system, there was this good practice and custom for the commander of the police and for the chief of the police station, as the political boss, do not belong to the same ethnic group; they would invariably be from different ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is absolutely correct. I know, in the former Communist system, there was this parity principal. So if a Bosniak was the number-one man, the number-two man should be a Serb, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that at the first multi-party elections in 1990, there was not only a change of regime, but also a change of system?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were not a member of any one of these newly-established parties; right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I was never a member of any political party from that day onwards until the present. I was only a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you and to remind myself that we should make shorter breaks between our questions and answers so that we do not make life too difficult for the interpreters. So between our questions and answers, short breaks.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that when the system was changed, people who came to power, especially at local level, were people who had never been in any position of authority before?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's the case, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that at some point in one of your statements; for example, that Ratko Radic had been a mechanic, and that later on you came to realise that these people who were in power, even if they wanted to, could not have done any better?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. He was a car repairman, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the elections, the Serb Democratic Party left policemen from the previous system at various posts in the police system, although practically none of them were members of the SDS; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: That is the case, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that it's not only that you were not a member of the SDS, but, rather, you were critical towards the new system, you criticised it, but nevertheless you remained in the position that you had held?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: That's right. Already then, I had clashed with the powers that be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the Party of Democratic Action, nevertheless, brought new people to hold these positions, people who had never worked for the police before?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree, and you confirmed that in your interview as well, that towards the end of 1991, there were certain abuses on the part of the Muslims, in terms of staffing within the police force?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that, for example, in this joint MUP, among 40 policemen, there were only a few Serbs?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Just a small correction. There were 45 members of the Public Security Station. Out of them, eight were Serbs, also there were three Croats, and all the rests were Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the level of the city, at the level of other municipalities in the city, were you aware of even more drastic examples, especially as far as the reserve force was concerned? For example, in the municipality of Stari Grad, they took in about 1.000 reserve policemen, out of which only 30 were Serbs? Not 30 per cent, but 30, so that would be 3 per cent .

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, I was aware of the situation precisely in Stari Grad. That was the most drastic of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that a source of great trepidation and uncertainty among the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At your local level and also throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, although you did not work for the State Security but for the Public Security, rather, did you have any information about other kinds of abuse, about the transport of weapons, about illegal arming, and so on?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name Senaid Memic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I know the name, because in Hadzici, already in January and February, we had absolutely accurate information about the distribution of weapons by parts of the SDA headed by Hasan Cengic. The gentleman you are referring to was in charge of procuring and distributing weapons for the municipalities within the city; among others, primarily the municipality of Hadzici, where I was first the commander and then the chief of the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that response. I think that in all these statements so far, no one asked you about Cengic, Memic, the Green Berets, the Patriotic League and so on. As a policeman, did you hear from your colleagues that the Patriotic League was being established with its headquarters in each and every municipality, and also with units of their own that had a command structure?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, we knew that, absolutely, and we knew that one of the ways in which weapons were being procured was precisely through this so-called military wing of the Party of Democratic Action. The Patriotic League grew out of that later. We knew that, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D52, can I ask for that, please. That's an exhibit, and we'd like to call it up in e-court. 1D52.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know or do you agree that Hasan Cengic was a clergyman?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could all the participants please cast a glance at this document. Actually, can we have the English version removed for now so that the witness can have a better look at the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear in the police that Hasan Cengic, though a cleric, had an important role --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we can't read B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. We'll try to remove the Serbian version from e-court and to provide the witness with a hard copy in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you find out in the police force that this Hasan Cengic played a very important role among the police, although he was not a policeman, in a very strange way; for instance, that he sent policemen to Croatia for training, Muslim policemen to Croatia, surreptitiously?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, and not only that. We know, with full reliability, that it was precisely that gentleman, with many of his co-workers, abused official IDs of the former Ministry of the Interior. This was classical abuse, and in that way they procured and distributed weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you now please have a look at this statement of Senaid Memic from Hrasnica. This statement was given on the 14th of April, 1992, after he was arrested, in proceedings related to the illegal transportation of weapons. I would like to ask all the participants to have a look at this document. Does this correspond with your own knowledge about the activities of this group, especially this man who was arrested and who gave this statement to the state authorities?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Just one small addition to this. I don't see a signature here on this document, but I'm sure -- judging by the style, I'm more than sure that it must have been someone from State Security in Ilidza. However, I've already said that as for this information that is contained in this document, we already knew about that in Hadzici. I have very, very concrete things that I know that can be linked to this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you give us a few facts that were well known to the police, if not generally known?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we knew that large-scale arming was already taking place amongst the Muslim Bosniak population in several ways, and one of the ways is the way that is being referred to in this document. Then there was this other way. At the time, they considered that to be legal; that is to say, they increased the number of members of the reserve force. They rapidly increased their numbers, especially in Tarcin. And towards the end of May 1992, these two stations had over 600 members. According to peacetime establishment, these two stations were supposed to have about 100 members, so the increase was six-fold. As for this specific knowledge, we had certain territories in the municipality of Hadzici. However, in view of the fact that the ethnic make-up of that station was as I had already described, I had a relatively small number of policemen, so we could not cover all of that. One day in February 1992, we were chasing each other, literally, all over Hadzici. With the representatives of the Bosniak police and the Bosniak municipal authorities of Hadzici, we had information that lots of weapons were being brought in from the direction of Mostar. We tried to stop that vehicle, and we were obstructed very seriously by our colleagues, so this vehicle escaped in the direction of Mokrin. Mokrin is outside Hadzici, and its population was predominantly Bosniak. Of course, as the then police commander, I informed certain authorities in writing about all of this. So within a day or two, an appropriate commission came to Hadzici of the then City Secretariat of the Interior of Sarajevo, headed by Goran Macar, who at the time was the head of the Police Department, and I know that Mr. Simo Tusevljak [phoen] also came. At the time, he was one of the top operatives in the territory of the city. They interviewed some policemen who were ethnic Bosniaks, and, inter alia, they directly linked my then deputy commander with this; namely, the distribution of that particular contingent. What I'm saying now must be contained in some of the archives of the City Secretariat, and there is a possibility of some traces being even in the archives of the Hadzic Police Station.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think Your Honours have already ruled in previous instances when Dr. Karadzic has endeavoured to tender statements, and I think that this is no different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Even if approved by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That approval was so vague as to not be of any assistance to anyone. The witness's comment was, if I recall it correctly, one of the methods described in this document, which is a four-page document full of detailed information, so, frankly, we don't know what the witness is referring to or talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We disagree. Given this is a 14 April 1992 statement taken during the course of a police investigation, it stands on the same footing as many of the Prosecution exhibits which have been admitted concerning shelling incidents, sniping incidents, which contain accounts from witnesses interviewed during the course of that immediate investigation, and we do think that the witness has more than agreed with the contents of this document and said that it accords with his information and he has additional information. So we think that it falls within your guide-lines and should be admitted, to be given whatever weight you believe it's entitled to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How are we to be satisfied as to the authenticity of this document, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe the witness, when he first saw the document, expressed that he could tell from the format of this document that this is exactly material coming from the State Security Bureau, so I believe he's given some weight to its authenticity. And if the Prosecution has any objection to its authenticity or concerns about it, then perhaps that would be more of an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the time being, we'll mark this for identification, and we'll come back to this issue very soon in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be MFI D1051.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Glavas, in order to make it clear for the participants: You mentioned Tarcin, Binjezevo, Pazarici and other places, and the place where this truck loaded with fire-arms escaped. Is it correct that Tarcin, Binjezevo, Pazarici and other places were large neighbourhoods that were parts of Hadzici municipality?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: That's correct, and that applies to all the places that you mentioned. Tarcin, Pazarici, Binjezevo were large settlements, and each such settlement was exposed of a number of villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did Tarcin and Pazaric have reserve police stations that grew up to 600 reserve policemen?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted the participants to know that this was happening in your municipality. Is it true that the Serbian part of the police realised that that was a way towards creating a single entity republican army?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Single ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was absolutely clear. If I may elaborate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: In that community, as well as elsewhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Serbs were a minority, so everybody knew that the Bosniak authorities tried to increase the number of reserve police officers as much as possible because, as I said, they perceived it as one of the ways to effect additional arming of their population. On the other hand, through the reserve police force, a comprehensive strategy was implemented, in terms of indoctrinating the reserve policemen, with a view to imparting on them that the only way for the Muslims to remain in a single Bosnia-Herzegovina as a majority, for them to be in a privileged position, but that the main obstacle on the road to that goal would be the Serbs. So they applied this kind of education of the reserve force, and at a later stage they used them as a kind of infrastructure for additional indoctrination of the entire Muslim population and, of course, for procuring additional fire-arms. So this is my interpretation as the root cause of violent conflicts between the Serbian population and the Muslim population, which sparked virtually overnight, and that was due to the indoctrination that I just spoke about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, going back to the previous document, which is Senaid Memic's statement which we marked for identification - I'm just speaking and asking for myself - if such a statement, a third person's statement, is to be admitted, then will the Prosecution be at liberty to tender hundreds of third-person statements when the witness confirms the content of those statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm wondering if the Chamber is reading my mind, because I was thinking, myself, that this is a slippery slope that we're going down. On the other hand, the Prosecution has already included, in its exhibits, and already been allowed to admit contemporaneous statements of investigations conducted at the time which relate to the events which are part of this trial, so I think that it has to be decided, perhaps, on an individual basis. But you're correct that it potentially can be damaging to the Defence, as well as beneficial to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you remind me of examples of admitting contemporaneous statement of investigation conducted at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: One thing that comes to mind right now is the shelling in Dobrinja of the 1st of June, 1993, when people were interviewed about what kind of shells fell and what calibre they were. I remember an individual named Dinko Bakal [phoen] saying that he found 60-millimetre shells at the scene of that Dobrinja incident, and that was contained in the police reports. So that's one that comes to mind immediately, and I think in other shelling incidents, in particular, and perhaps sniping incidents, they are contained in those police reports, interviews of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll be able to give Your Honours the exhibit number for that very quickly, but that was contained within an UNPROFOR report investigating the incident and part of the index of supporting material to the ultimate final report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come back to that issue. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add, this is not a statement. This document is part of the police investigation process. That would be all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, is it true --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you are not giving your evidence, so you can call a witness who is able to give what the document is about. Let's proceed. Refrain from making a statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. All I wanted was to be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that there was another way of arming people? In other words, is it true that in your municipality, the Muslim part of the police force appropriated joint weapons even by resorting to breaking into the depots where these common weapons were kept?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. In late March of 1992, while we were still operating as a single public security station, in which I was the commander, Fado Covic was the chief, and, as I said, in late March of 1992, we provided physical security for the central depot of the former Ministry of the Interior in Rakovica, which means that it was within the area of responsibility of my station. The then deputy of mine prepared a rota in which he included only Bosniaks, and this infamous breaking in or, rather, an assault of Rakovica took place that night. The Green Berets came and transported everything that could have been found in that depot, including weapons and police equipment, vehicles, combat vehicles, police cars -- everything was transported across Mount Igman. Since I said that I had a relatively small number of officers at my disposal, was exposed to severe criticism from the people who were in charge of the CSB and the politicians in charge of Hadzici and Ilidza, unfortunately objected. Simply speaking, I could not have done more than I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that you were the only one -- the only Serb who attended senior staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Speaking about the inner circle of the senior staff, I attended, but if it was a wider circle, Branislav Mijatovic attended as well. But on most occasions, I was the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that before the police was divided and before the Serbian MUP was formed, the police executives in Hadzici would come alongside, and they were wearing green berets on their head, and you asked them that whilst they were still in the police, they should follow the dress code and dress properly?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. At the time when the police station was still functioning as a joint institution, I was the commander of that police station. And by virtue of my position, I commanded the entire police force in Hadzici. That refers to members of active-duty policemen and reserve policemen as well. I had the misfortune at the time that all reserve policemen were Bosniaks, and this was particularly prominent with the heads of Tarcin and Pazaric police stations, who, during those turbulent times, came to meetings with green berets on their heads. At one of these meetings, I was very vocal, and I told them that I would not allow them to come to meetings with green berets for as long as I was the commander of the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm for the transcript that the commanders of the reserve force were Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's all going very fast, Your Honour, and Dr. Karadzic is speaking before the witness's answers are concluded, let alone translated. So I wonder if everybody could be cautioned to slow their pace a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm only amazed by the talents of our excellent interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please put a pause between the question and answers, and please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We owe a lot to our interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that before the depot was robbed, the depot was run by a Serb named Boro who was dismissed from this position before the robbery, i.e., towards the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, but I have to correct you. When I spoke about the breaking in to the central depot in Rakovica, I have to say that we also had our own internal depot at the level of the police station. It is true that Mr. Boro Suvajlo [phoen] was in charge of all the materiel and equipment. When Mr. Fadil Covic and I took our positions, we found him already there. After these events, the Bosniak police officers started protesting and telling me that they resent the fact that he was a Serb, and that they were afraid that he would be impartial. I offered a solution, and we decided to replace Boro with a Croat. So since they had an objection to this, I tacitly accepted their protest, and we appointed this Croat. However, this was followed by infamous events related to the division of the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It seems to me that the joint depot was in Hadzici, and the one in Rakovica was at republican level. Actually, it was for the entire MUP of the republic. Right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like us to deal with the few things that were, indeed, of a political nature. However, you must have followed them too, and they did affect the police as well. Is it correct that Muslims and Croats were political allies, in view of having Bosnia separated from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: You really have to repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that, politically speaking, before the war both Muslims and Croats, or, rather, their leading political parties, were in favour of secession, the secession of Bosnia from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Ah, yes, that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This attempt to establish republican armies through the MUP, and increasing the reserve force, and so on and so forth, did that remind you of the establishment of republican armies in Slovenia and Croatia? Was that the same path that had been taken?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, the very same scenario, but in a different way, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But President Tudjman could say, at an early stage, This was the National Guards Corps, right, so that was a type of police as well; right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really think that this is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the Serb side accepted, with great difficulty and involving great pains, that Bosnia be separated from Yugoslavia and reorganised?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in many municipalities in which conditions were right for that, there were negotiations underway on the reorganisation of municipalities into two; namely, Serb neighbourhoods and Serb parts of that particular town would be a Serb municipality, whereas Muslim neighbourhoods and Muslim parts of town would be a Muslim municipality?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that, and I can try to demonstrate that using the example of the environment that I functioned in. As for Hadzici, there were several attempts to have agreement reached between the two sides, along the lines that you refer to just now, to carry out a division of the territory - perhaps I could put it that way - as follows: The Serbs would be in charge of the area that had a predominantly Serb population, whereas the areas where there was a predominantly Muslim population would be under their authority. As for Ilidza and the security service there, I know about that. I know that the then head, Edim Livic, and Mr. Tomislav Kovac, who was the police commander, they had agreed that policemen of Bosniak ethnicity carry out work from the domain of our service in the area of Hrasnica and in other predominantly Muslim-populated areas, whereas ethnic Serb policemen carried out the same kind of work in the area of Ilidza, where the population was predominantly Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that on the 18th of March, an agreement was reached, and it is well known as the Lisbon Agreement or, rather, the Cutileiro Plan?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. But, Mr. Karadzic, I'd like to ask you something. If possible, please don't put questions like that to me, because these questions, more or less, have to do with high-level politics. I was never a politician. I was just an ordinary policeman. I don't know whether I can give answers to such questions. If you put questions to me in a certain context, I can give answers about what I know about, but please do not ask me about high-level politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. You are quite right. But I wanted to ask you: When the police was divided, did you realise that the essence of the Lisbon paper was that we would have our own police? If you don't know about that, never mind.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I knew that. It was a generally-known thing, the Lisbon Agreement, and then the denial of that Lisbon Agreement. That's something everyone knows about, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that when two municipalities are established, two police stations are established as well?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that not necessarily all of them, but that most Muslim policemen would go to their own police station and most of the Serb policemen to their own police station?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: That's the way it was supposed to be, but, unfortunately, that is not what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Although this is an assumption, but had there not been a war, would Hadzici ever have two municipalities within its structure, like many other towns do?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I believe that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the Serb side? Was there a consolidation of sorts that happened, and were weapons obtained as well?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Yugoslav People's Army was in Bosnia until the 20th of May?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the JNA particularly interested in its own infrastructure in Hadzici, that is, the Technical Institute, and the Zunovnica depot, and other military facilities there?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There's quite a few questions here that are calling for speculation, and I think that's another one. How on earth is this witness to know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If he knows. Can you answer the question, Mr. Glavas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, I did understand Mr. Karadzic's question, and I do agree. These were areas that the JNA aspired for, and they had reason to try to keep that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the local population, the local structures, were not happy with the fact that the army was focusing only on its own facilities and were not guarding the municipality as a whole?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: They were absolutely unsatisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the army had a shortage of manpower because Muslims and Croats did not respond to mobilisation or call-up?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: That's right, and that is a generally-known thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the army believed that the Serbs would respond, if necessary, and that, in return, they did provide some -- they did take some measures to ensure the safety of the Serb neighbourhoods in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in the previous system, reservists could take their equipment home, weapons included?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: In the previous system, that was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Those who were asked to come to military exercises, didn't they take their uniforms home, and some even took their automatic weapons home?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: You were not clear enough. Are you referring to the reservists of the former JNA or are you referring to the reservists of the police force?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The JNA reservists.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Well, that's a different matter, and that possibility did exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Seeing and knowing what was happening within the Muslim community, did you try to do something about providing weapons to the Serb community through reserve policemen or in some other way?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: I could do very little. And, specifically, I was never involved in this distribution of weapons. However, as for part of the police reserve force, I armed them with an additional supply from the former Zunovnica Barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can one say that the police divided peacefully in many municipalities and, by way of agreement, also the basic equipment and weapons were divided, as well as vehicles, and that you, as the minority community in Hadzici, fared rather poorly, in terms of this division of equipment?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, we fared catastrophically, because we had far fewer members because of that ethnic balance and due to the fact that, objectively speaking, I could not keep the headquarters of the Public Security Station at the location where it was. I had to go to various improvised locations. So, of course, I could not get any of those weapons, except for a few members of the reserve police force who had taken their weapons with them and who were Serbs, I mean. As for vehicles, I only had one single vehicle, the one that I drove as the then police commander. I took that vehicle and perhaps a few of those radios that were used for communication, and that is what we had at that point in time at the police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just noting that that was a compound question, and the witness has confined his answer to the second part of the compound question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you reach an agreement to separate, after talks that were held, in accordance with the divisions of the police in other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS
