utterances.text: I could not agree that we had had some kind of agreement, but I remember full well that this was sometime in the first half of April 1992. When the then chief of the Public Security Station, Mr. Fadil Colic [as interpreted], called me to the police station, I came with eight other members of the police force who were ethnic Serbs. The subject discussed at that meeting was the relations among the police force at the Public Security Station in Hadzici. Of course, Mr. Fadil Colic, in view of the post that he held, made certain introductory remarks, saying that we were moving on, as was the case before, that they were the legal representatives of the police authorities in that area, and all of this took a normal course until I asked for the floor. Of course, what I said irritated everyone there, because this is what I said: Gentlemen, do you see what happened in all neighbouring municipalities, I said, in Stari Grad, in Novo Sarajevo, in the centre, in Pale, Sokolac, Vogosca, Ilijas? There were splits along ethnic lines, and the police was divided in all of these locations that I refer to. That same thing would have to happen here, where we are, and now it is a question of common sense and wisdom as to how this should be carried out. My intention was to do things in a civilised manner, if I can put it that way, for us to go our separate ways in a civilised way, if it can be put that way. However, there is nothing I could do at that meeting, because my remarks caused a vociferous reaction among the Muslim Bosniak police. One of the policemen got up, and I'm telling you literally what happened. He went to the door of the room where we were meeting. He took a hand-grenade from his pocket, and he stood in front of me, having taken the fuse out, and he said, You cannot leave this room until we resolve these problems. Dragan Krstic, a policeman who was with me, and who was very brave in such situations invariably, he took out a hand-grenade as well and did the same thing. Since he was good friends with this other policeman, who was an ethnic Bosniak, he said, No problem, friend. If necessary, we are all going to die. Only thanks to the composure of some of the policemen who were there, Bosniaks, I have to say, who respected me, who held me in high regard even in that situation, they -- one of them got up, grabbed him by the chest, took him from the door, and said, What on earth are you doing? Are we all supposed to be killed here? So it was a most unfortunate situation. I left the joint premises then, and this was practically the definite separation between the two police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The killing of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll stop here for today. It's time. There are, briefly, two matters to deal with before we rise today. As regards the Defence motion/request to have Dr. Subotic during the testimony of a ballistic expert, I think it's straightforward. We'll grant it, but it remains to be seen whether or not he will, indeed, testify. And the second matter relates to the Prosecution's submission. Mr. Tieger, Friday you told us about a couple of witnesses whose testimony is fixed to certain dates. You are not going to file separately in writing?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Having provided that information in court, we didn't intend to. We're certainly prepared to do so, if the Court wishes, but that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary. But as regards the second witness, who was fixed, according to your submission, to 14th to 16th, originally 14th March was not a date on which we were supposed to sit. I think the March calendar -- it's because the March calendar hasn't been produced yet. But is it possible to sit from 15th, instead of 14th?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may. Your Honour, the witness is an under-secretary-general who is involved in logistics for most of the United Nations missions overseas, so all I can say is I'll communicate with his staff immediately and do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Glavas, we'll adjourn for today and resume tomorrow. But there's one witness the cross-examination of whom couldn't be concluded due to shortage of time last week, so tomorrow morning we'll begin with that witness, and your testimony will probably resume around 1.00, probably during the third session. Thank you for your understanding. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Excuse me, Mr. President. I would like to make a motion that the pleadings concerning Mr. Zecevic be unsealed at this time. And I've spoken with the Prosecution about that, and perhaps Mr. Gaynor could address you on that, but I think that this is the appropriate time now for those matters to be made public.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, subject only to the observation that there is a medical report in the documentation provided by the Bosnian authorities which does contain information which is essentially personal medical details of Mr. Zecevic. The rest of it, we have no objection to it becoming public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just out of an abundance of caution, we'll communicate it from out of the courtroom. We are now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 15th of February, 2011, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.34 p.m.,
